headline: Dreams might be your brain's way of processing emotions, solving problems, and rehearsing possibilities
universal_truth: The mind works on problems even when you're not aware; trust the process
fun_facts: You forget 95% of your dreams within 5 minutes of waking
Everyone dreams—people who say they don't simply don't remember them
The strange logic of dreams happens because your prefrontal cortex (rational thinking) is largely offline during REM sleep
discussion_questions: Why are dreams so strange and illogical?
Have you ever solved a problem in a dream?
What might your recurring dreams mean?

hook.script: Every night, you experience vivid hallucinations that feel completely real—then forget almost all of them. Dreams seem meaningless, but they might serve crucial functions: processing emotions, consolidating memories, even rehearsing threats. Why does your brain create these nightly movies?

cliff.script: Dreams are universal—every human dreams, even if they don't remember. But what's the purpose of these strange nocturnal experiences?

options.text: Dreams may help process emotions, consolidate memories, and simulate scenarios—your brain working through problems while you sleep
options.response: Yes. Multiple theories suggest dreams serve real functions—emotional regulation, memory processing, threat rehearsal. The brain isn't idle; it's working differently.

options.text: Dreams are random brain activity that doesn't serve a purpose
options.response: Some scientists proposed this, but evidence suggests dreams do serve functions...

fact1.title: Emotional Processing
fact1.script: Dreams often feature emotionally significant content. REM sleep may help process and regulate emotions—people deprived of dream sleep become more emotionally reactive. Dreams might be therapy you give yourself every night.

fact2.title: Problem Solving
fact2.script: Many discoveries came in dreams: the structure of benzene, the sewing machine, songs and stories. While you sleep, your brain makes connections your waking mind misses. 'Sleep on it' is literally good advice.

fact3.title: Threat Simulation
fact3.script: Most dreams involve negative emotions—anxiety, fear, threat. One theory: dreams are rehearsals for danger, letting you practice responses safely. Nightmares might be training simulations your brain runs for survival.

wisdom.script: Here's today's wisdom: The mind works on problems even when you're not aware. Dreams teach that trusting the process means trusting work you can't see. Solutions often arrive when you stop consciously trying.

outro.script: That's Day 132. Tomorrow, we'll explore where food comes from. Until then, keep a notebook by your bed—capture dreams before they fade. You might discover your sleeping mind is working on something.

growTrack.title: Dream Journal - Capture the Unconscious
growTrack.activity: Keep paper by your bed. When you wake, immediately write whatever you remember—even fragments. After a week, look for patterns: recurring themes, emotions, situations. Your dreaming mind might be telling you something your waking mind doesn't want to hear.
